opening.headline: Solve the problem of images growing large and build secrets remaining in the image using multi-stage builds and secret mounts, and learn how to read model declarations and GPU reservation settings in Compose.
body: Let's say you built the service as a container, the image grew to several GB, and you added a token for private package access as a build argument. After uploading the image to the registry, anyone could see the token in the layer history. An image is a snapshot of the moment it was created, so once entered, the file remains in the previous layer even if you later delete it.

In this class, we first look at small base images, multi-stage builds, and how to reduce images and build contexts with .dockerignore. Next, check the path where the build secret is left in the layer and how to block it with a secret mount, and read the structure of Compose's models element, Docker Model Runner, and GPU reservation settings. Compare whether model weights should be placed in an image, mounted as a volume, or downloaded at startup, and even check how the container uses the host's GPU. At the end, we explain compose settings that cause GPU reservation errors.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of multi-stage builds, tags, and build secrets
Analyze what model declarations and GPU reservation settings in Compose mean
Methods of including model weights in the image, mounting them as a volume, and downloading them at startup can be compared in terms of image size and startup time.
Describe the roles played by the host driver and container runtime for a container to use the host's GPU.

screens.lead: Select the layers in the picture one by one from top to bottom to see where each layer's added files and tokens remain.

items.answer: All builds start from a base image. The larger the base image, the larger the production image. Base image affects download speed and number of vulnerabilities.

When you install a compiler and development headers to build a package, these tools remain in the production image. This file is not used when the service runs, but increases the image size and attack surface.

items.prompt: Layer 3: Token added as build argument
items.answer: If you pass a token as a build argument to access a private package, the build argument and environment variables remain in the final image. Even if you delete a file from a later layer, the history of this layer will not be lost.

items.prompt: Result: After uploading to the registry
items.answer: When you upload an image to the registry, anyone who can receive the image will see the token in the layer history. It is necessary to destroy the token and reissue it. Both size and secrecy problems stem from the lack of distinction between the build process and the production image.

screens.outro: Now that we know what the problem looks like, let's think about a similar experience.

screens.title: Think about it: What's in the image?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: The image grew larger and the build secret remained in the image. Have you ever seen a similar situation?
items.answer: Secret problems are often discovered while reducing image size. Both problems stem from the same root: lack of control over what goes into the image.

items.prompt: Which files are really needed in the production image, and which are only needed for build?
items.answer: All that is needed for execution is application code, runtime, dependent libraries, and model files. The compiler, test tools, and package cache are only needed for builds. Expressing this division as stages in a Dockerfile is a multi-stage build.

items.prompt: Do you know where the settings go when moving a service that uses GPUs to a container?
items.answer: GPU access is declared not in the Dockerfile, but in the run configuration, i.e. in the deploy entry of the compose file. Even if the image is the same, how many GPUs are reserved on which host is determined at execution time.

screens.outro: First, let's look at how to make an image smaller.

screens.title: Dockerfile best practices and multistage
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to see how the final image changes in terms of tooling and size.

visual.alt: A bar diagram comparing the sizes of a single-stage image and a multi-stage image.

states.label: single stage
states.body: One FROM handles both build and execution. The compiler, source, and build intermediate artifacts all remain in the final image, resulting in a larger image and more vulnerabilities. When choosing your main image, it's a good idea to choose a smaller image from a trusted source. This is because the smaller it is, the faster it is to download and the fewer vulnerabilities it has. Tags can point to different content over time, so you need to be clear about which version they are.

states.label: multi stage
states.body: Divide your Dockerfile into build steps and final steps. Compilation and package installation are completed in the build stage, and only the output required for execution is copied in the final stage. No build tools remain in the final image, reducing its size. You create common components into reusable steps, so Docker builds the common steps only once. Images are immutable, meaning they are a snapshot of the moment they were created and must be rebuilt regularly. `--pull` receives a newer base image even if it is cached locally, and `--no-cache` recreates all layers from scratch.

screens.outro: Now that we have control over the content inside the image, let's see how to control the files sent to the build.

screens.title: .dockerignore: Remove from context
screens.lead: Below is an example of a .dockerignore file. Select the underlined lines to see what each pattern takes away from the build context.

marks.note: This is a local environment file that contains secrets. If taken out of context, there is no way to accidentally enter the image with the COPY command.
This is the local data folder. When large files are included in the context, transfer times increase each time a build is started and the cache is unnecessarily broken each time data changes.

This is the model weight file. You need to be intentional about whether you want to include it in the image or mount it separately; if you include it without intention, it will greatly bloat the image. The criteria for this selection will be compared in the very next screen.
The exclamation point indicates an exception to the preceding pattern. All markdown is removed with *.md, but only README.md is left in the context. Pattern syntax similar to .gitignore.

screens.outro: Now that we've reduced the context, let's see how to prevent the secret from leaving a path in the image.

screens.title: Three ways to pass model weights to the container
screens.lead: Read the table and compare the methods of adding weights to the image, mounting them as volumes, and downloading them at startup. Notice how the image size, transfer, and start time vary in each column.

data.caption: Comparison of model weight transfer methods
columns: Start time of new pod or container
rows: Included in image
It's inside the image layer. Put it as COPY in the Dockerfile.
The image becomes larger by the weight size. Nodes download only the layers they do not have and reuse the layers they already have.
If the image already exists on the node, there is no download time. For new nodes without images, the time to receive a full image is added.
This is suitable when the weights do not change frequently and the same results must be reproduced by distributing only one image.
volume mount
This is storage outside of the image. Compose mounts the host path, and Kubernetes mounts it as a volume such as PersistentVolumeClaim.
The image contains only the code and runtime, keeping it small. If the storage allows reads from multiple places, multiple pods share the same weight.
There are no download steps. Instead, the speed at which files are read from storage is factored into model loading time.
It is suitable when the weights are large, the model is changed frequently, and the same weights are read by multiple containers.
Download at startup
This is temporary storage inside a container. The startup script or init container takes it from the model repository and places it in a volume such as emptyDir.
The image is small, but it transmits weights every time a new pod pops up.
The contents of emptyDir are cleared when a pod is removed from a node, so they are re-received for each new pod. Of the three methods, this has the longest startup time.
It is suitable for services where weights are versioned in a separate repository and startup delays are not an issue.
data.notes: Let's say your weight file is 16GB. If you put it in an image, it should get a 16GB layer every time a pod pops up on a new node that doesn't have an image. However, if you place the line that copies the weight in the Dockerfile before the line that copies the code that changes frequently, the weight layer will remain the same in the new image with only the code changed, so the node will not receive it again. Downloaded at startup, this transfer is repeated each time the pod pops up. Either way, model loading time for uploading files to memory or GPU is separate. The sum of these times is the time it takes for the service to be ready to receive a request, and is the basis for determining the allowable time for status checking and the waiting time when the service first comes in without a request. Also, keep in mind that the mounted path obscures the contents of the same path in the image, and if you only want to read the weights, it is safer to mount it with the read-only option.

screens.outro: Now that we've decided where to place the weight, let's take a look at the path the secret takes during the build.

screens.title: Path where the build secret is left in the layer
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the path the secret takes and whether or not there is a trace left in the image.

tabs.label: Build arguments and environment variables
tabs.body: The values passed as `ARG` and `ENV` remain in the final image. So the documentation explains that build parameters and environment variables are not suitable for passing secrets. If you check the image layer history, the values ​​will remain visible and will not disappear from the previous layer even if you delete them in a later step.

tabs.label: secret mount
tabs.body: A secret mount provides the build client's secret as a file to the build container only while the corresponding `RUN` command is running. Usage is two steps. First, pass the secret to the build command like `docker build --secret id=aws,src=$HOME/.aws/credentials .`. Then use it as `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=aws` in your Dockerfile. The default path is `/run/secrets/<id>` and can be changed to another file name or environment variable with the `target` option. The source of the secret is a file or environment variable.

tabs.label: SSH mount
tabs.body: SSH mount temporarily provides an SSH socket or key when pulling a private Git repository during a build. Like a secret mount, no key is left on the image layer. This method is suitable for builds that require sources from private repositories.

tabs.label: Git authentication
tabs.body: When building a private Git repository as a remote context, there is a predefined secret. This secret is not used in the build command; it is a preparatory secret that provides the credentials the builder needs to obtain context.

screens.outro: Now let's read the structure of declaring a model in Compose.

screens.title: Compose models and Docker Model Runner
screens.lead: The compose file below is an example of declaring a model as part of the app composition. Select a range of lines from the description on the right to read what each part means.

data.code:
services:
  chat-app:
    image: my-chat-app
    models:
      llm:
        endpoint_var: AI_MODEL_URL
        model_var: AI_MODEL_NAME
      embedding-model:
        endpoint_var: EMBEDDING_URL
        model_var: EMBEDDING_NAME

models:
  llm:
    model: ai/smollm2
    context_size: 1024
    runtime_flags:
      - "--a-flag"
  embedding-model:
    model: ai/all-minilm

notes.note: Connect models by placing a models item in the service. By using long syntax, you can directly specify the name of the environment variable that the service receives. Here AI_MODEL_URL, AI_MODEL_NAME, EMBEDDING_URL, EMBEDDING_NAME are created. In the short syntax, variables such as LLM_URL and LLM_MODEL are automatically created according to the model name.

You declare the model in the top-level models element. model is required and is the OCI artifact identifier. context_size is the maximum token context size, increasing it will increase the hardware burden, so leave only as much as you need. runtime_flags are command line flags that are passed as is to the inference engine.

You can declare multiple models. Models not used by the service are not connected, and environment variables are not created in the service just by declaration. This feature requires a supporting platform such as Compose and Docker Model Runner that understands the models element.

screens.outro: Now that we have declared our model, let's look at the structure of our GPU reservation settings.

screens.title: How GPUs are used in containers
screens.lead: Select the numbered markers in the picture to see how GPU access is divided between the host, container runtime, and container.

visual.alt: A layered structure diagram showing a container runtime and NVIDIA Container Toolkit on top of the host's kernel and GPU driver, and the two containers above that are connected to GPU devices.
labels: Host: Linux kernel, NVIDIA drivers, GPU
CDI specification file: device name, device node, mount, environment variables
Associate device files and driver libraries

markers.label: Host kernel and drivers
markers.title: GPU drivers are placed on the host
markers.body: Containers are not virtual machines, but isolated processes that share the host's kernel. The driver that controls the GPU operates in conjunction with the kernel, so it is installed on the host. The NVIDIA Container Toolkit's instructions also explain that the NVIDIA driver is required on the host, and the CUDA Toolkit does not need to be installed on the host. If the host doesn't have a driver, the container won't be able to see the GPU.

markers.label: inside the container
markers.title: Place applications and libraries in images
markers.body: Libraries such as CUDA used by the model server can be placed on the image side. So you can run images using different library versions together on the same host. However, the host driver and the library in the image must be compatible with each other, so if the two do not match, a GPU initialization error may occur.

markers.label: NVIDIA Container Toolkit
markers.title: Runtime configures container for GPU
markers.body: NVIDIA Container Toolkit is a collection of libraries and tools for creating and running GPU-enabled containers. It is linked to the container runtime and automatically configures the required GPU device and host driver-related files to be visible within the container when the container starts. Users do not copy drivers into the image.

markers.label: CDI
markers.title: Describe the device in a standard format
markers.body: Container Device Interface (CDI) is a specification that allows container runtimes to support third-party devices. A device has a fully qualified name in the form vendor.com/class=name, and container changes such as device nodes, mounts, environment variables, and hooks are written in a JSON or YAML specification file. The runtime finds a specification that matches the requested device name and applies it to the container settings. It is not within the scope of CDI to decide how much resources to give to whom, and that decision is made by the Orchestrator.

markers.label: declaration
markers.title: compose and manifest declare what to write
markers.body: Device reservations under deploy or GPU requests in Kubernetes only declare which GPUs to use and how many, and do not directly install drivers or connect devices. The actual connection is made by the host's driver and container runtime layers. If the declaration is correct but the GPU is not visible, check the host and runtime layers before the declaration file.

screens.outro: Now that we know the principle, let's read the fields that declare GPU reservations in compose one by one.

screens.title: Structure of GPU reservation settings
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined field in the text, you'll see what it means, whether it's required, and which fields can't be used together.

data.text: In Compose, GPU resources are declared in the order of deploy, resources, reservations, and devices. The devices field may include the following fields: driver, count, device_ids, capabilities, options. Among these, capabilities must be specified, and count and device_ids cannot be used simultaneously. If both are omitted, all GPUs on the host are used.

terms.tip: It is a list of strings, for example capabilities: [gpu]. This is a required field, and if it is not present, an error will occur when deploying.
Enter the number of GPUs to reserve as an integer or all. If omitted or all, all GPUs on the host will be used. Cannot be used with device_ids.
List of specific GPU device IDs on the host. Check the ID in the output of running nvidia-smi on the host. Cannot be used with count.
Write it as a string, for example driver: nvidia. Since the container shares the host's drivers, this value must match the GPU driver installed on the host.
This is a field where driver-specific options are written as key and value pairs.

screens.outro: Now that we know what the fields mean, let's read the error-producing settings ourselves.

screens.title: Commentary 1: Reading compose with GPU reservation error
screens.lead: `compose up` stops with an error in the devices section. Select the right arrow to follow the instructor's inspection sequence.

steps.title: View the settings in question
steps.body:
In the following settings, `docker compose up` stops with a devices entry error.

```yaml
services:
  inference:
    image: my-inference
    deploy:
      resources:
        reservations:
          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: 1
              device_ids: ["0"]
```

The error message points under devices, so check the fields in this entry one by one.

steps.title: Step 1: Do you have the capabilities?
steps.body: First, look for `capabilities` under devices. There are no capabilities in the above settings. This field must be set; if it is not present, an error will occur when deploying the service. This is the first cause.

steps.title: Step 2: Did you write down both count and device_ids?
steps.body: The above settings write down both count and device_ids. Both fields cannot be used at the same time; only one must be defined. To specify a specific device, leave only device_ids, and to specify only the number, leave only count. This is the second cause.

steps.title: Step 3: Driver and host environment
steps.body: Verify that the driver value matches the GPU driver installed on the host. Run `nvidia-smi` on the host to see if the driver is visible and the device ID is correct. The same symptom occurs even if the file is correct but the host is not ready.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: Modified settings are organized as `driver: nvidia`, `count: 1`, and `capabilities: [gpu]`. The order of checking is required fields, fields that cannot be used together, and host environment. If you start by looking at what can be checked within the file and check the external environment last, time will be reduced.

screens.outro: Next is a commentary on fixing the secret and size problems together.

screens.title: Commentary 2: Modifying secret and size together
screens.lead: Let's go back to the first problem and fix the Dockerfile with the remaining tokens and large image step by step. Select the right arrow to see what each modification changes.

steps.title: Before fixing
steps.body:
The steps of receiving the token as `ARG`, writing it to `pip install`, and installing the compiler remain in the final image.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12
ARG PRIVATE_TOKEN
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential
COPY . /app
RUN pip install -r /app/requirements.txt
```

The token is left in the layer history and the build tools are included in the production image.

steps.title: Step 1: Mount ARG incognito
steps.body: Remove `ARG` and read the token as `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=token`. When building, pass it as `docker build --secret id=token,src=./token.txt .`. The token exists as a `/run/secrets/token` file only during the RUN command and does not remain in the layer.

steps.title: Step 2: Divide the build stage and execution stage
steps.body: Separate the steps of installing the compiler and building the package into a build stage, and copy only the required output to `COPY --from` to the execution stage. You can also choose a smaller base image in the execution stage.

steps.title: Step 3: Reduce the context with .dockerignore
steps.body: Write `.env` and local data in `.dockerignore` to take it out of context. It blocks the path where files that should not be included in the image enter `COPY . /app` and reduces unnecessary cache damage.

steps.title: result
steps.body: Tokens disappear from the image layer history and build tools are removed from the final image, reducing its size. Tokens from previous images that have already been uploaded to the registry must be discarded and reissued. Fixing it doesn't make the already leaked values ​​safer.

screens.outro: Let me summarize the key points by combining the two cases.

screens.title: TL;DR: Images, secrets, and declaration structures
screens.lead: We will organize what we have seen so far into one standard.

paragraphs: With small base images and multi-stage builds, the final image contains only the files needed to run. Since the image is immutable, it is rebuilt regularly, and `--pull` and `--no-cache` are used for this purpose. `.dockerignore` reduces context and prevents files from being accidentally entered.

Secrets are not treated as build arguments, but as secret mounts or SSH mounts. Forward is `docker build --secret`, use is `RUN --mount=type=secret`. Since the value once entered into the layer cannot be returned, the solution is to block it.

Model weights can be placed in an image, mounted as a volume, or downloaded at startup. If you put it in an image, the transfer happens on a per-image basis, if you mount it, the image becomes smaller but the storage read speed is factored into the loading time, and if it downloads on startup, the transfer repeats for each new pod. Containers share GPU drivers with the host kernel, and tools in the container runtime connect devices to containers.

The models element in Compose declares a model as part of the app's composition. GPU reservation is declared in devices under deploy, capabilities are required, and count and device_ids cannot be used at the same time. You can read error messages by knowing the declaration structure and required fields.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The image contains only what is necessary for execution, secrets are borrowed only during the build, and configuration first checks required and mutually exclusive fields.

data.notes: If you omit both count and device_ids in GPU reservation, all GPUs on the host will be used, so it is safer to specify them intentionally on public hosts.

glossary.def: This method divides the build phase into the execution phase and contains only the files needed for the final image.
This is secret information needed only during the build. It is delivered without leaving an image with a secret mount.
This file contains file patterns to exclude from the build context. It uses a similar syntax to .gitignore.
This is the top-level element of the Compose file and is a way to declare AI model dependencies along with the service.
This is a setting that declares the GPU to be used by the service in devices under deploy. Capabilities are essential.
It is a collection of tools that configure device and driver-related files along with the container runtime so that the container can use the host's NVIDIA GPU.

misconceptions.myth: The secret passed to ARG disappears after the build is completed.
misconceptions.fact: Build arguments and environment variables remain in the final image. The secret must be passed through a secret mount or SSH mount so it does not remain in the layer.

misconceptions.myth: Once an image is created, it is always safe.
misconceptions.fact: An image is an immutable snapshot of a moment in time. It does not reflect updates to the base image and must be rebuilt regularly.

misconceptions.myth: You can specify the GPU more accurately by using count and device_ids together.
misconceptions.fact: Both fields cannot be used at the same time; only one must be defined. Use device_ids to specify a specific device, or count to determine the number.

misconceptions.myth: To use a GPU, you must also include a GPU driver in the image.
misconceptions.fact: Containers share drivers with the host kernel. Drivers install on the host, and tools in the container runtime connect the device to the container. The image contains the application and the libraries it uses.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Reduce the image to a small base image and multi-stage.
The secret is passed through the mount and is not left in the layer.
Compose models declares a connection between a model and a service.
The GPU driver is placed in the host, GPU reservation requires capabilities, and count and device_ids cannot be used at the same time.
Model weights are selected based on size and startup time among image inclusion, volume mount, and download at startup.
